summary: Okanogan NF lookout above Harts Pass. 1931 L-4 cab; 1954 ground cab; top 40 ft cut for an Air Force radar in 1956; 41-ft tower; collapsed winter 2026. Road closed; remains not described.

facts.design: L-4 cab on a 41-foot treated-timber tower (current structure, 1956)
facts.status_note: Collapsed in the winter of 2026 (firelookout.com). WillhiteWeb says a windstorm blew the tower over in early 2026; MVFFLA gives no cause.

staffing.status: not staffed; abandoned for a number of years before the collapse

access.note: MVFFLA says Harts Pass Road was significantly damaged and will be closed by the Forest Service until repairs are complete. Visitors are asked to honor closures and avoid disturbing the site.

events.note: Reported first structure: a gable-roof cupola cabin. WillhiteWeb says it may never have existed.
Gable-roofed L-4 cab built; first telephone line strung to the summit the same year
Peak occupied for the first time (1931 item quoted by Weebly); Ed Allen and Raymond Johnson were completing the lookout house, then it was staffed for the rest of the season
Lightning bolt damaged the roof, disrupted the telephone and set the lookout's bed afire
Hip-roofed L-4 ground cab placed on the summit. Register and WillhiteWeb say it came from Leecher Mountain; firelookout.com says that cab went to Twisp
Air Force took the summit for a gap-filler radar station; cab removed and top 40 feet of the peak cut away. Firelookout.com dates this 1956 with a question mark, possibly later
Current structure: L-4 cab on a 40/41-foot timber tower (MVFFLA lists 1956 as the current structure build year; WillhiteWeb says the cab went back up between 1956 and 1960)
Radar station declared excess in January; sold by bid for salvage, including the radar tower, by October
Mr. and Mrs. Jon Shepard were the lookouts; they left near the end of the season and Al Anderson of Winthrop finished it
Pressed into emergency service when nearby Goat Peak Lookout had to be evacuated for fire
Used to monitor the Elbow Basin fire in the Pasayten Wilderness and relay radio messages
Tower collapsed over the winter (firelookout.com: winter of 2026; WillhiteWeb: windstorm in early 2026)

corrections.why: The register describes the lookout on a 41-foot tower and firelookout.com describes a 41-foot timber tower, about 12.5 m. 53 m would be about 174 feet, which no source gives.
MVFFLA reports damage to Harts Pass Road and a Forest Service closure until repairs are complete.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources give a 1924 cupola (doubted), a 1931 L-4 cab, a 1954 ground cab, and the current structure of 1956. The record's 1956 date refers to the current structure, which fits MVFFLA. The earlier stages are kept as separate events.
The register gives 7,308 ft (2,227 m); firelookout.com gives 7,440 ft. The record's 2,227.5 m follows the register.
The register, MVFFLA and WillhiteWeb say the L-4 came from Leecher Mountain. firelookout.com says that cab went to Twisp for a Civil Air Defense lookout instead.
The register says the radar station was never built. firelookout.com says it was partly completed before being declared obsolete. WillhiteWeb says the radar tower was sold for salvage in 1961.
WillhiteWeb says a windstorm blew the tower over in early 2026. MVFFLA and firelookout.com report a winter collapse without naming a cause.

notes_for_editor: Built, staffing and radar history are well covered by four sources that mostly agree; the disputes are listed in resolved_conflicts. The 2026 collapse is confirmed by firelookout.com and WillhiteWeb, but the MVFFLA cached text has no year and gives no cause. Current site condition is not described by any page read, so the story says so. MVFFLA's intro text says the summit was blasted in 1926, which contradicts its own 1956 history; I treated 1926 as an error. Unread leads from search snippets, not used: Methow Valley News (2026-04-02) on the collapse and access; TrailChick (a March 11, 2026 storm). Reads used: 6 distinct pages (NHLR, MVFFLA news, MVFFLA page, firelookout.com, Weebly, WillhiteWeb). Weebly and WillhiteWeb were each re-read once with --grep because the first 3,000-character read cut off the Slate Peak text, so there were 8 fetch calls in total. Searches: 1.
